Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings  
• Unilateral (left) sensorineural-type hearing difficulty, facial numbness, tinnitus, and intermittent dizziness, subacute onset (3 weeks).  
• No otalgia, discharge, fever, dysphagia, dysarthria, limb weakness, or vision change.  
• Family history of neurofibromatosis increases risk for vestibular schwannoma.  

Working diagnosis  
1. Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) – most likely given unilateral auditory symptoms, facial sensory involvement, and NF in first-degree relative (DDx “High”).  
2. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – possible but less consistent (sensory > motor, hearing loss present; DDx “Medium”).  

Considerations  
• Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Low-Medium) – less likely due to absence of pain or vesicular rash.  
• Central lesions (brainstem stroke, demyelination) – low probability but would require exclusion if exam abnormal.  

Management  
• Urgent same-day face-to-face GP assessment requested for full neurological and otoscopic examination.  
• Plan for prompt ENT/Neurology referral and MRI internal auditory canals if vestibular schwannoma suspected.  
• If Bell’s palsy confirmed clinically, initiate corticosteroids within 72 h of onset (outside window; discuss risks/benefits).  
• Advise patient that presentation is unlikely life-threatening but needs timely evaluation.  
• Provide clinic contact number; patient instructed to attend today.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Vestibular schwannoma – High likelihood: Progressive unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, facial numbness; NF in sibling raises risk.  
2. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – Medium likelihood: Unilateral facial sensory change without systemic features; however lacks classic motor palsy.  
3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome – Low–Medium likelihood: Could explain triad but absent pain/rash decreases probability.
